questions.title: What is the purpose of the DOCTYPE declaration in HTML5?
questions.description:
DOCTYPE Declaration

The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration is the first line of an HTML document. It tells the browser which version of HTML the page is written in, ensuring the browser renders the page in standards mode rather than quirks mode.

Key Points

  • In HTML5, the DOCTYPE is simply <!DOCTYPE html>
  • It is not an HTML tag; it is an instruction to the browser
  • Without it, browsers enter quirks mode, causing inconsistent rendering
  • It must appear before the <html> tag
questions.bestPractices:
• Always include <!DOCTYPE html> as the very first line of every HTML document
  • Use lowercase letters for consistency
  • Do not include any whitespace or comments before the DOCTYPE
questions.commonMistakes:
• Omitting the DOCTYPE entirely, which triggers quirks mode
  • Using outdated XHTML or HTML 4 DOCTYPE declarations
  • Placing comments or whitespace before the DOCTYPE
  • Thinking DOCTYPE is an HTML tag
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My Page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello World</h1>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to gauge if you understand browser rendering modes. Emphasize the difference between standards mode and quirks mode, and how the DOCTYPE prevents layout inconsistencies across different browsers.

questions.title: Explain the basic structure of an HTML5 document and the role of each essential element.
questions.description:
HTML5 Document Structure

A well-formed HTML5 document consists of several essential elements that define the document's structure and metadata.

Essential Elements

  • <!DOCTYPE html> - Declares the document type
  • <html> - Root element wrapping all content
  • <head> - Contains metadata, title, styles, scripts
  • <meta charset="UTF-8"> - Sets character encoding
  • <meta name="viewport"> - Controls responsive behavior
  • <title> - Defines the page title shown in browser tabs
  • <body> - Contains all visible content
questions.bestPractices:
• Always specify lang attribute on <html> for accessibility
  • Place <meta charset> as the first element in <head>
  • Include viewport meta tag for responsive design
  • Keep title concise but descriptive
questions.commonMistakes:
• Forgetting the lang attribute, impacting screen readers
  • Placing <meta charset> after other elements
  • Omitting the viewport meta tag, breaking mobile layouts
  • Having multiple <title> tags
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Accessible Web Page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
  </header>
  <main>
    <p>Content goes here.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Demonstrate that you understand the semantic meaning of each element, not just memorization. Highlight how proper document structure impacts accessibility, SEO, and maintainability.
followUpQuestions: Why is the lang attribute important on the html element?

questions.title: What are meta tags and which meta tags are essential for modern web development?
questions.description:
Meta Tags

Meta tags provide metadata about the HTML document. They are placed inside the <head> element and are not visible to users but are used by browsers, search engines, and other web services.

Essential Meta Tags

  • Charset: <meta charset="UTF-8"> - Defines character encoding
  • Viewport: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> - Enables responsive design
  • Description: <meta name="description" content="..."> - Used by search engines for snippets
  • Robots: <meta name="robots" content="index, follow"> - Controls crawling and indexing
questions.bestPractices:
• Always include charset and viewport meta tags
  • Write unique, compelling meta descriptions for each page (under 160 characters)
  • Use Open Graph meta tags for social media sharing
  • Include theme-color meta tag for browser UI customization on mobile
questions.commonMistakes:
• Forgetting the viewport meta tag, leading to mobile rendering issues
  • Using duplicate meta descriptions across pages, hurting SEO
  • Putting meta tags in the body instead of the head
  • Using outdated meta tags like keywords for SEO purposes
questions.example:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <meta name="description" content="Learn modern web development with practical examples and best practices.">
  <meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Web Development Guide">
  <meta property="og:description" content="Learn modern web development.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/image.jpg">
  <meta name="theme-color" content="#ffffff">
</head>
questions.interviewTip: Show awareness of both SEO and social sharing implications. Mention Open Graph (Facebook) and Twitter Cards. Discuss how the viewport meta tag is crucial for responsive web design.

questions.title: What is semantic HTML? Compare semantic and non-semantic elements with examples.
questions.description:
Semantic HTML

Semantic HTML uses elements that convey meaning about the content they contain. They clearly describe their purpose to both the browser and the developer.

Semantic vs Non-Semantic

Semantic ElementsNon-Semantic Elements
<header>, <footer><div>
<article>, <section><span>
<nav>, <main><div class="nav">
<aside>, <figure><div class="sidebar">

Semantic elements improve accessibility for screen readers, boost SEO by helping search engines understand content structure, and make code more maintainable.
questions.bestPractices:
• Use <header>, <main>, and <footer> for page-level structure
  • Use <article> for self-contained content
  • Use <section> for thematic grouping of content with a heading
  • Use <nav> for primary navigation links
  • Use <aside> for tangentially related content
questions.commonMistakes:
• Overusing <div> when a semantic element exists
  • Using <section> as a generic container without a heading
  • Wrapping everything in <article> unnecessarily
  • Nesting <main> inside another semantic element like <article>
questions.example:
<!-- Non-semantic -->
<div class="header">
  <div class="nav">...</div>
</div>
<div class="content">...</div>
<div class="footer">...</div>

<!-- Semantic -->
<header>
  <nav>...</nav>
</header>
<main>
  <article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
    <p>Content...</p>
  </article>
</main>
<footer>...</footer>
questions.interviewTip: Emphasize the triple benefit of semantic HTML: accessibility (screen readers), SEO (search engines), and developer experience (readable code). Be ready to name at least 10 semantic elements and explain when to use each.

questions.title: Explain the purpose and correct usage of heading elements (h1-h6) in HTML.
questions.description:
Heading Elements

Heading elements (<h1> through <h6>) define the hierarchical structure of content. <h1> represents the highest level, and <h6> the lowest.

Key Principles

  • Use only one <h1> per page for the main title
  • Maintain a logical hierarchy: don't skip levels (e.g., h1 to h3)
  • Headings should describe the content that follows
  • Screen readers use headings to navigate content via heading landmarks
questions.bestPractices:
• Use a single <h1> that matches the page's primary topic
  • Organize headings in a logical nested order without skipping levels
  • Keep heading text descriptive and concise
  • Style headings with CSS rather than choosing a heading level based on appearance
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using multiple <h1> tags on a single page
  • Skipping heading levels (e.g., going from <h2> to <h4>)
  • Choosing heading levels based on font size rather than semantic meaning
  • Using headings for purely stylistic purposes on non-heading text
questions.example:
<!-- Correct heading structure -->
<h1>Web Development Guide</h1>
  <h2>Frontend Technologies</h2>
    <h3>HTML Basics</h3>
    <h3>CSS Styling</h3>
    <h3>JavaScript Fundamentals</h3>
  <h2>Backend Technologies</h2>
    <h3>Node.js</h3>
    <h3>Python</h3>

<!-- Incorrect: Don't skip levels -->
<h1>Main Title</h1>
  <h3>Subtitle</h3> <!-- Skipped h2 -->
questions.interviewTip: Emphasize the accessibility and SEO importance of proper heading hierarchy. Mention that screen reader users often navigate by headings (pressing 'H' key). The HTML5 outline algorithm was intended to support multiple h1s in sections, but it was never fully implemented, so stick to one h1.

questions.title: What are the main semantic structural elements introduced in HTML5 and when should you use each?
questions.description:
HTML5 Semantic Structural Elements

HTML5 introduced several semantic elements that provide meaning to the structure of a web page beyond simple <div> containers.

Key Semantic Elements

  • <header> - Introductory content or navigational links for a page or section
  • <footer> - Closing content for a page or section (copyright, links, author info)
  • <nav> - Primary navigation blocks
  • <main> - The dominant content of the document (unique to the page)
  • <article> - Self-contained, independently distributable content
  • <section> - Thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading
  • <aside> - Content tangentially related to the main content (sidebars, callout boxes)
questions.bestPractices:
• Use exactly one <main> per page
  • Use <article> for blog posts, news articles, comments, or widgets
  • Use <section> only when content has a natural heading
  • Use <nav> for major navigation blocks, not every link group
  • Multiple <header> and <footer> elements are allowed within sections
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using <section> as a generic container instead of <div>
  • Wrapping the entire page in an <article>
  • Placing <main> inside <article> or <aside>
  • Using multiple <nav> elements for minor link groups
questions.example:
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>My Blog</h1>
    <nav>
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main>
    <article>
      <h2>Blog Post Title</h2>
      <p>Post content...</p>
      <section>
        <h3>Comments</h3>
        <!-- Comment list -->
      </section>
    </article>

    <aside>
      <h3>Related Posts</h3>
      <ul>...</ul>
    </aside>
  </main>

  <footer>
    <p>© 2024 My Blog</p>
  </footer>
</body>
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the WAI-ARIA landmark roles that these elements map to (header -> banner, nav -> navigation, main -> main, footer -> contentinfo). Mention that proper use of these elements creates an accessible page outline automatically for screen readers.

questions.title: What are text-level semantic elements in HTML and how do they improve content meaning?
questions.description:
Text-Level Semantic Elements

Text-level elements add meaning to inline content, helping assistive technologies and search engines understand the emphasis and significance of text fragments.

Common Text-Level Elements

  • <strong> - Indicates strong importance, seriousness, or urgency
  • <em> - Indicates stress emphasis, changing meaning subtly
  • <mark> - Highlights text for reference or notation purposes
  • <cite> - References a creative work's title
  • <time> - Represents a specific time or date
  • <abbr> - Abbreviation or acronym with optional title attribute
  • <code> - Inline code snippet
  • <kbd> - Keyboard input
  • <small> - Side comments or fine print
  • <del> and <ins> - Deleted and inserted content
questions.bestPractices:
• Use <strong> for content of strong importance, not just bold styling
  • Use <em> for emphasis that changes the sentence meaning, not just italic styling
  • Always include datetime attribute on <time> when possible
  • Use <abbr> with a title attribute explaining the abbreviation
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using <b> and <i> when <strong> and <em> are more semantically appropriate
  • Nesting <strong> inside <strong> — each level increases importance, but it's rarely needed
  • Using <u> for non-hyperlink text, which can confuse users expecting links
  • Forgetting datetime attribute on <time> elements
questions.example:
<p>
  The event is on
  <time datetime="2024-12-25">December 25th, 2024</time>.
  <strong>Registration is required.</strong>
</p>
<p>
  I <em>really</em> think you should attend.
  Read <cite>The Design of Everyday Things</cite>.
  Use <code>console.log()</code> to debug.
  Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save.
</p>
<p>
  <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is the standard.
  <mark>This text is highlighted</mark> for reference.
  The price was <del>$10</del> <ins>$8</ins>.
</p>
questions.interviewTip: Distinguish between presentational elements (b, i) and semantic elements (strong, em). Screen readers may change their tone for em content but not necessarily for i. Understanding the nuanced difference shows deeper HTML knowledge.

questions.title: How do you create accessible navigation using HTML landmarks and proper link structure?
questions.description:
Accessible Navigation

Accessible navigation ensures all users, including those using screen readers or keyboard-only navigation, can easily find and navigate through site content.

Key Components

  • Landmark Elements: Semantic HTML5 elements (<nav>, <main>, <header>, <footer>) automatically create ARIA landmarks
  • Skip Links: "Skip to main content" links help keyboard users bypass repetitive navigation
  • Descriptive Link Text: Avoid "click here" — use meaningful link text
  • Current Page Indicator: Use aria-current="page" to identify the active link
questions.bestPractices:
• Wrap primary navigation in a <nav> element with an accessible label using aria-label if there are multiple navs
  • Provide a visible focus indicator (outline) for keyboard users
  • Ensure all interactive elements are keyboard accessible
  • Use aria-current="page" on the link representing the current page
  • Implement skip navigation links that become visible on focus
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using non-descriptive link text like "click here" or "read more"
  • Removing focus outlines with outline: none without providing alternatives
  • Creating navigation with <div> elements instead of <nav>
  • Not labeling multiple <nav> elements, causing confusion for screen reader users
questions.example:
<!-- Skip link -->
<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>

<header>
  <nav aria-label="Primary navigation">
    <ul>
      <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
      <li><a href="/about">About Us</a></li>
      <li><a href="/services">Our Services</a></li>
      <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>

<main id="main-content">
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>Page content...</p>
</main>

<footer>
  <nav aria-label="Footer navigation">
    <ul>
      <li><a href="/privacy">Privacy Policy</a></li>
      <li><a href="/terms">Terms of Service</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</footer>
questions.interviewTip: Mention the 'Tab' key navigation pattern and how skip links work with CSS (visually hidden until focused). Discuss landmark navigation in popular screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) — users can press 'D' to jump between landmarks.

questions.title: What is the difference between ordered, unordered, and description lists in HTML? Provide examples of appropriate use cases.
questions.description:
HTML Lists

HTML provides three types of lists, each serving different semantic purposes and rendering with distinct default styles.

List Types

  • Unordered List (<ul>): A collection of items where order doesn't matter. Rendered with bullet points by default.
  • Ordered List (<ol>): A sequence of items where order matters. Rendered with numbers or letters by default.
  • Description List (<dl>): A list of terms and their descriptions. Uses <dt> for the term and <dd> for the description.
questions.bestPractices:
• Use <ul> for navigation menus, feature lists, or any unordered collection
  • Use <ol> for step-by-step instructions, recipes, or rankings
  • Use <dl> for glossaries, metadata displays, or FAQ sections
  • Nest lists when creating hierarchical structures
  • Use CSS list-style to customize appearance instead of changing list type
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using <ol> when order isn't meaningful, confusing screen readers
  • Using <br> tags to simulate list items instead of proper list elements
  • Using <dl> for general key-value pairs that aren't truly term-description relationships
  • Forgetting to close list item <li> tags
questions.example:
<!-- Unordered List -->
<h2>Shopping List</h2>
<ul>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
</ul>

<!-- Ordered List -->
<h2>How to Boil Water</h2>
<ol>
  <li>Fill pot with water</li>
  <li>Place on stove</li>
  <li>Turn on heat</li>
  <li>Wait for bubbles</li>
</ol>

<!-- Description List -->
<h2>Glossary</h2>
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language - structure of web pages</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets - presentation of web pages</dd>
</dl>

<!-- Nested Lists -->
<ul>
  <li>Frontend
    <ul>
      <li>HTML</li>
      <li>CSS</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Backend</li>
</ul>
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the semantic meaning conveyed to assistive technologies: screen readers announce 'list with 3 items' for ul/ol and provide navigation shortcuts (L key). For ol, screen readers announce the item number and total count. Description lists announce the number of terms.

questions.title: How do you create accessible and well-structured tables in HTML?
questions.description:
Accessible HTML Tables

HTML tables should be used exclusively for tabular data, never for layout. Accessible tables provide proper structure so screen readers can convey relationships between cells.

Table Structure

  • <table> - The table container
  • <caption> - Table title or description (appears above the table)
  • <thead> - Header rows group
  • <tbody> - Body rows group
  • <tfoot> - Footer rows group
  • <th> - Header cell (use scope attribute)
  • <td> - Data cell
questions.bestPractices:
• Always include a <caption> to describe the table's purpose
  • Use <th> with scope="col" or scope="row" to associate headers with data cells
  • Group rows with <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot>
  • For complex tables, use headers and id attributes to associate cells with multiple headers
  • Never use tables for page layout — use CSS Grid or Flexbox instead
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using tables for layout purposes instead of CSS
  • Omitting <th> elements or not using scope attributes
  • Forgetting the <caption> element
  • Not indicating the relationship between header and data cells
  • Using nested tables for complex layouts
questions.example:
<table>
  <caption>Quarterly Sales Report (2024)</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Product</th>
      <th scope="col">Q1 Sales</th>
      <th scope="col">Q2 Sales</th>
      <th scope="col">Q3 Sales</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Widget A</th>
      <td>$10,000</td>
      <td>$12,000</td>
      <td>$15,000</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Widget B</th>
      <td>$8,000</td>
      <td>$9,500</td>
      <td>$11,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Total</th>
      <td>$18,000</td>
      <td>$21,500</td>
      <td>$26,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
questions.interviewTip: Screen reader users navigate tables with special commands (Ctrl+Alt+Arrow keys in NVDA). When they move between cells, the screen reader announces the associated header. Using proper scope attributes makes this possible. Mention responsive table patterns for mobile (horizontal scroll wrapper, data attribute technique, or converting to cards).

questions.title: Explain the anatomy of an anchor element. What are the different values for the target attribute and their implications?
questions.description:
The Anchor Element

The <a> (anchor) element creates hyperlinks to other pages, files, locations within the same page, email addresses, or any URL-addressable resource.

Key Attributes

  • href - The destination URL (required for a link)
  • target - Where to open the linked document
  • rel - Relationship between current and linked document
  • download - Prompts download instead of navigation
  • hreflang - Language of the linked resource

Target Values

  • _self (default) - Open in same window/tab
  • _blank - Open in new window/tab
  • _parent - Open in parent frame
  • _top - Open in full body of the window
questions.bestPractices:
• Always use rel="noopener noreferrer" with target="_blank" for security
  • Use descriptive link text — avoid "click here"
  • Indicate when a link opens in a new window (visually or via aria-label)
  • Use absolute URLs for external links, relative URLs for internal links
  • Ensure links are keyboard focusable and have visible focus styles
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using target="_blank" without rel="noopener", creating security vulnerability (tabnabbing)
  • Using non-descriptive link text like "click here" or "read more"
  • Empty href attribute (href="") which links to the current page
  • Using href="#" for JavaScript-only links instead of a <button>
questions.example:
<!-- External link with security best practices -->
<a href="https://example.com"
   target="_blank"
   rel="noopener noreferrer">
  Visit Example
  <span class="sr-only">(opens in new tab)</span>
</a>

<!-- Internal relative link -->
<a href="/about">About Us</a>

<!-- Email link -->
<a href="mailto:contact@example.com">Email Us</a>

<!-- Telephone link -->
<a href="tel:+15551234567">Call (555) 123-4567</a>

<!-- Link to page section (fragment) -->
<a href="#section2">Jump to Section 2</a>

<!-- Download link -->
<a href="/files/report.pdf" download>Download Report</a>
questions.interviewTip: Be sure to mention the tabnabbing attack: when a page opens a link with target="_blank", the new page can access window.opener and potentially redirect the original page to a phishing site. rel="noopener" prevents this by setting window.opener to null.

questions.title: How do you work with images in HTML? Cover the img element, responsive images, and accessibility considerations.
questions.description:
Images in HTML

Images are a fundamental part of the web. Proper implementation ensures they are accessible, performant, and responsive across devices.

The img Element

  • src - Image source URL
  • alt - Alternative text (required for accessibility)
  • width and height - Intrinsic dimensions (prevents layout shift)
  • loading="lazy" - Defers loading until near viewport

Responsive Images

  • srcset - List of image candidates for different resolutions/widths
  • sizes - Media conditions to tell browser which image size to select
  • <picture> - Art direction and format switching
questions.bestPractices:
• Always provide meaningful alt text (empty alt="" for decorative images)
  • Specify width and height to prevent Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
  • Use loading="lazy" for below-the-fold images
  • Provide multiple resolutions via srcset and sizes
  • Use modern formats (WebP, AVIF) with <picture> for fallback
questions.commonMistakes:
• Omitting the alt attribute or using it incorrectly
  • Using massive, unoptimized images that slow page load
  • Not specifying width and height, causing layout shifts
  • Using CSS to resize large images instead of serving appropriately sized images
  • Forgetting to provide fallback formats in the picture element
questions.example:
<!-- Basic responsive image -->
<img src="photo-800.jpg"
     alt="Sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w,
             photo-800.jpg 800w,
             photo-1200.jpg 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw,
            (max-width: 900px) 50vw,
            33vw"
     width="800"
     height="600"
     loading="lazy">

<!-- Art direction with picture -->
<picture>
  <source srcset="hero-wide.avif" type="image/avif" media="(min-width: 768px)">
  <source srcset="hero-wide.webp" type="image/webp" media="(min-width: 768px)">
  <source srcset="hero-mobile.avif" type="image/avif">
  <img src="hero-fallback.jpg" alt="Team collaborating in a modern office">
</picture>

<!-- Decorative image -->
<img src="decorative-border.png" alt="" role="presentation">
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the performance benefits of width/height attributes (modern browsers calculate aspect ratio to reserve space before load, reducing CLS). Explain the difference between resolution switching (srcset with x or w descriptors) and art direction (picture element with media queries). Mention decoding="async" attribute for off-main-thread image decoding.

questions.title: Explain the HTML5 picture element and its use cases for art direction and format switching.
questions.description:
The Picture Element

The <picture> element provides flexibility for specifying image resources based on media queries, device pixel ratios, or supported image formats. It contains <source> elements and one fallback <img> element.

Use Cases

  • Art Direction: Display different image crops or compositions at different viewport sizes
  • Format Switching: Serve modern formats (WebP, AVIF) to supporting browsers with fallbacks
  • Resolution Switching: Provide different resolutions for different screen densities (though srcset on img may suffice)
questions.bestPractices:
• Always include a fallback <img> element as the last child
  • Place <source> elements in order of preference (most preferred first)
  • Use media attribute for art direction scenarios
  • Use type attribute for format switching (e.g., image/webp, image/avif)
  • Still include alt text on the fallback <img> for accessibility
questions.commonMistakes:
• Forgetting the fallback <img> element entirely
  • Putting alt on <source> elements instead of the <img>
  • Reversing the order of <source> elements (first match wins)
  • Using <picture> when simple srcset on <img> would suffice
questions.example:
<picture>
  <!-- WebP for browsers that support it -->
  <source srcset="hero-desktop.webp"
          type="image/webp"
          media="(min-width: 768px)">
  <source srcset="hero-mobile.webp"
          type="image/webp">

  <!-- Fallback JPEGs -->
  <source srcset="hero-desktop.jpg"
          media="(min-width: 768px)">
  <source srcset="hero-mobile.jpg">

  <!-- Ultimate fallback -->
  <img src="hero-fallback.jpg"
       alt="Company team photo with diverse employees"
       width="1200"
       height="630">
</picture>
questions.interviewTip: The browser evaluates each source element in order and selects the first one that matches. Only one image is downloaded. This is critical to understand — the order of sources matters. Mention that for simple resolution switching, srcset on img is often simpler and more appropriate than picture.

questions.title: What are the key attributes of the img element for performance and why are they important?
questions.description:
Performance Attributes for img

Modern HTML provides several attributes on the <img> element that significantly impact page performance, user experience, and Core Web Vitals metrics.

Key Performance Attributes

  • loading - Controls when images are fetched (eager or lazy)
  • fetchpriority - Hints to the browser which images to prioritize (high, low, auto)
  • decoding - How the browser should decode the image (sync, async, auto)
  • width and height - Intrinsic dimensions for aspect ratio calculation
  • srcset and sizes - Responsive image selection
questions.bestPractices:
• Use loading="lazy" for images below the fold
  • Use fetchpriority="high" for LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) images
  • Always specify width and height to prevent layout shifts
  • Use decoding="async" for off-main-thread decoding of non-critical images
  • Combine srcset and sizes to serve appropriately sized images
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using loading="lazy" on above-the-fold images, delaying LCP
  • Omitting width and height, causing Cumulative Layout Shift
  • Setting fetchpriority="high" on too many images, diluting its effect
  • Not using decoding="async" for large off-screen images
questions.example:
<!-- Hero image (LCP) - load eagerly with high priority -->
<img src="hero.jpg"
     alt="Main promotional banner"
     fetchpriority="high"
     loading="eager"
     width="1200"
     height="600">

<!-- Below-fold content image - lazy load with async decoding -->
<img src="article-photo.jpg"
     alt="Article illustration"
     loading="lazy"
     decoding="async"
     width="800"
     height="450"
     srcset="article-photo-400.jpg 400w,
             article-photo-800.jpg 800w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw">

<!-- Low-priority decorative image -->
<img src="background-texture.png"
     alt=""
     fetchpriority="low"
     loading="lazy"
     width="200"
     height="200">
questions.interviewTip: Connect these attributes to Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) improves with eager loading and high fetchpriority on hero images; CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) is prevented by width/height; overall load performance improves with lazy loading. Mention that lazy loading has a distance threshold — browsers load lazy images when they're within a certain distance of the viewport, not just when visible.

What is the difference between decoding sync and async?

questions.title: What are the different types of image formats for the web and when should you use each?
questions.description:
Web Image Formats

Choosing the right image format balances visual quality, file size, and browser support. Modern formats offer superior compression, but require understanding of fallback strategies.

Common Formats

  • JPEG: Lossy compression, 16M colors, no transparency. Best for photographs.
  • PNG: Lossless compression, supports transparency. Best for logos, icons, images requiring transparency.
  • GIF: Limited to 256 colors, supports animation. Best for simple animations (though outdated).
  • SVG: Vector format, infinitely scalable. Best for icons, logos, illustrations.
  • WebP: Modern format with lossy/lossless compression, transparency, animation. ~25-35% smaller than JPEG/PNG.
  • AVIF: Next-gen format, even better compression than WebP. Best quality-to-size ratio, but limited browser support.
questions.bestPractices:
• Use WebP or AVIF with JPEG/PNG fallbacks via <picture>
  • Use SVG for icons, logos, and vector graphics
  • Use JPEG for photographs when modern formats aren't supported
  • Use PNG for images requiring precise transparency that WebP/AVIF can't handle
  • Avoid GIF — use animated WebP or video (MP4/WebM) instead
questions.commonMistakes:
• Serving unoptimized, full-resolution images directly from a camera
  • Using PNG for photographs (can be 5-10x larger than JPEG)
  • Using GIF for video clips (can be 10-20x larger than equivalent MP4)
  • Not providing modern format with fallbacks
  • Rasterizing SVGs into PNG when they could be served as vectors
questions.example:
<!-- Modern format with fallback -->
<picture>
  <source srcset="photo.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="photo.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="photo.jpg" alt="Scenic mountain landscape">
</picture>

<!-- Inline SVG for icons -->
<svg width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">
  <path d="M12 2L2 7l10 5 10-5-10-5z" fill="currentColor"/>
</svg>

<!-- Animated WebP as GIF replacement -->
<img src="animation.webp" alt="Product demonstration animation">
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the size comparisons: AVIF can be 50% smaller than JPEG at equivalent quality, WebP about 25-35% smaller. Mention that Safari added WebP support relatively late (2020) and AVIF support even later (2023). Discuss the importance of the picture element's type attribute for format selection — the browser downloads only the first matching format it supports.

questions.title: How do you create accessible forms in HTML? Cover labels, fieldsets, error handling, and ARIA.
questions.description:
Accessible Forms

Accessible forms ensure that all users, including those using assistive technologies, can understand, navigate, and complete form inputs successfully.

Key Components

  • Labels: Every input must have an associated <label> (explicit using for/id or implicit wrapping)
  • Fieldsets and Legends: Group related form controls with <fieldset> and <legend>
  • Error Messages: Associate error messages with inputs using aria-describedby
  • Required Fields: Indicate required fields with both visual indicator and required attribute or aria-required
  • Instructions: Provide clear instructions using aria-describedby linking to help text
questions.bestPractices:
• Always use explicit label association (<label for="id">) for maximum compatibility
  • Group radio buttons and checkboxes within <fieldset> with a <legend>
  • Provide clear, specific error messages placed near the problematic input
  • Use aria-describedby to connect inputs with error/help text
  • Ensure focus order is logical and matches visual order
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using placeholder text as a substitute for labels
  • Not programmatically associating error messages with inputs
  • Forgetting to group related radio buttons in a fieldset
  • Using color alone to indicate required fields or errors
  • Not providing visible focus indicators on form controls
questions.example:
<form novalidate>
  <!-- Grouped fields -->
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Contact Information</legend>

    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="name">Full Name</label>
      <input
        type="text"
        id="name"
        name="name"
        required
        aria-describedby="name-help name-error"
      >
      <span id="name-help">Enter your first and last name.</span>
      <span id="name-error" role="alert" class="error" hidden>
        Name is required.
      </span>
    </div>

    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="email">Email Address</label>
      <input
        type="email"
        id="email"
        name="email"
        required
        aria-describedby="email-error"
      >
      <span id="email-error" role="alert" class="error" hidden>
        Please enter a valid email address.
      </span>
    </div>
  </fieldset>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Preferred Contact Method</legend>
    <input type="radio" id="contact-email" name="contact" value="email">
    <label for="contact-email">Email</label>

    <input type="radio" id="contact-phone" name="contact" value="phone">
    <label for="contact-phone">Phone</label>
  </fieldset>

  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
questions.interviewTip: Emphasize that placeholder text fades out and is not a substitute for a label. Discuss the difference between aria-labelledby (overrides the label) and aria-describedby (supplements with additional info). Mention how role="alert" on error containers makes screen readers immediately announce dynamic error messages.

questions.title: What are the different input types in HTML5 and how do they improve user experience?
questions.description:
HTML5 Input Types

HTML5 introduced many specialized input types that go beyond the basic text type. These provide appropriate on-screen keyboards on mobile devices, built-in validation, and semantic meaning.

Common HTML5 Input Types

  • email - Optimized for email addresses with built-in validation
  • url - For URLs with protocol validation
  • number - Numeric input with stepper controls
  • tel - Telephone numbers (triggers numeric keypad on mobile)
  • date, time, datetime-local - Date/time pickers
  • search - Search fields with clear button
  • color - Native color picker
  • range - Slider control
  • password - Masked input
questions.bestPractices:
• Use type="email" for email fields — triggers email keyboard on mobile
  • Use type="tel" for phone numbers — triggers numeric keypad
  • Use type="number" only for quantities, not for IDs or credit card numbers
  • Combine with inputmode attribute for finer keyboard control
  • Always provide server-side validation in addition to browser validation
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using type="number" for credit card numbers, postal codes, or phone numbers
  • Relying solely on client-side validation without server-side checks
  • Forgetting that type="number" allows scientific notation (e.g., 1e5)
  • Not testing date inputs across browsers — implementation varies significantly
questions.example:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email"
         placeholder="you@example.com">

  <label for="phone">Phone</label>
  <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone"
         pattern="[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}"
         placeholder="555-123-4567">

  <label for="quantity">Quantity (1-10)</label>
  <input type="number" id="quantity" name="quantity"
         min="1" max="10" step="1" value="1">

  <label for="birthdate">Date of Birth</label>
  <input type="date" id="birthdate" name="birthdate"
         min="1900-01-01" max="2024-12-31">

  <label for="site">Website</label>
  <input type="url" id="site" name="site"
         placeholder="https://example.com">

  <label for="color">Favorite Color</label>
  <input type="color" id="color" name="color" value="#ff0000">

  <label for="volume">Volume</label>
  <input type="range" id="volume" name="volume"
         min="0" max="100" value="50">
</form>
questions.interviewTip: Highlight the mobile UX improvements: type="email" brings up a keyboard with @ symbol; type="tel" brings up a numeric keypad; type="date" uses the native device date picker. Mention the inputmode attribute as a complementary tool when you want a specific keyboard without the semantic implications of a type.

questions.title: Explain HTML5 form validation attributes and how to create custom validation messages.
questions.description:
HTML5 Form Validation

HTML5 provides built-in form validation through attributes and a JavaScript Constraint Validation API. This reduces the need for custom validation libraries for basic cases.

Built-in Validation Attributes

  • required - Field must be filled before submission
  • pattern - Regex pattern the value must match
  • min / max - Minimum and maximum values for numeric/date inputs
  • minlength / maxlength - Character length constraints
  • type - Built-in validation for email, URL, number, etc.

Constraint Validation API

  • checkValidity() - Returns true if valid
  • reportValidity() - Checks validity and shows browser's default error
  • setCustomValidity(message) - Sets custom error message
  • validity - ValidityState object with detailed error flags
questions.bestPractices:
• Use novalidate on the form and implement custom validation UI for consistency
  • Always provide server-side validation as a security layer
  • Use setCustomValidity('') to clear a previously set custom error
  • Combine HTML5 validation with custom JavaScript for complex rules
  • Provide clear, specific error messages that help users fix the issue
questions.commonMistakes:
• Relying on browser default validation UI, which varies across browsers
  • Forgetting to call setCustomValidity('') after fixing a custom error
  • Using pattern without explaining the expected format to users
  • Not testing validation on different browsers and devices
questions.example:
<form id="signup" novalidate>
  <label for="username">Username (3-20 characters, letters and numbers only)</label>
  <input
    type="text"
    id="username"
    name="username"
    required
    pattern="[a-zA-Z0-9]{3,20}"
    minlength="3"
    maxlength="20"
  >

  <label for="password">Password (min 8 chars, 1 uppercase, 1 number)</label>
  <input
    type="password"
    id="password"
    name="password"
    required
    minlength="8"
    pattern="(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*[0-9]).{8,}"
  >

  <button type="submit">Create Account</button>
</form>

<script>
const form = document.getElementById('signup');

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  if (!form.checkValidity()) {
    event.preventDefault();
    // Custom validation logic
    const username = document.getElementById('username');
    if (username.validity.valueMissing) {
      username.setCustomValidity('Username is required.');
    } else if (username.validity.patternMismatch) {
      username.setCustomValidity('Username must be 3-20 characters, letters and numbers only.');
    } else {
      username.setCustomValidity('');
    }
    form.reportValidity();
  }
});

// Clear custom validity on input
form.addEventListener('input', (event) => {
  event.target.setCustomValidity('');
});
</script>
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the ValidityState object properties: valueMissing, typeMismatch, patternMismatch, tooLong, tooShort, rangeUnderflow, rangeOverflow, stepMismatch, badInput, customError. Each maps to a specific constraint. Show that you understand when to use HTML5 validation vs custom validation — HTML5 for simple constraints, custom for complex business rules and consistent UX.

questions.title: How do you structure complex forms with multiple sections, conditional fields, and multi-step workflows?
questions.description:
Complex Form Structure

Complex forms require careful planning of the HTML structure, navigation, state management, and accessibility to ensure users can complete them successfully.

Key Techniques

  • Fieldsets for Sections: Group related fields using <fieldset> with <legend>
  • Multi-Step Forms: Break long forms into manageable steps with progress indicators
  • Conditional Fields: Show/hide fields based on previous selections
  • Data Persistence: Save partial progress to avoid data loss
  • Navigation: Clear back/next buttons with validation at each step
questions.bestPractices:
• Use <fieldset> elements to visually and semantically group sections
  • Implement a progress indicator (steps, percentage, etc.)
  • Validate each step before allowing progression
  • Use aria-live regions to announce dynamic content changes
  • Save form state to localStorage/sessionStorage for recovery
  • Manage focus: move focus to the first field of a new step or to error summary
questions.commonMistakes:
• Not announcing step changes to screen reader users
  • Losing user data when navigating between steps
  • Not providing a way to go back and edit previous steps
  • Showing all errors at the end instead of step-by-step
  • Conditional fields that are not keyboard accessible
questions.example:
<form id="multi-step-form" novalidate>
  <!-- Progress indicator -->
  <ol class="progress-steps" aria-label="Form progress">
    <li class="active">Personal Info</li>
    <li>Address</li>
    <li>Review</li>
  </ol>

  <!-- Step 1: Personal Info -->
  <fieldset class="form-step" data-step="1">
    <legend>Personal Information</legend>

    <label for="fullname">Full Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="fullname" name="fullname" required>

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

    <label for="employment">Employment Status</label>
    <select id="employment" name="employment">
      <option value="">Select...</option>
      <option value="employed">Employed</option>
      <option value="self-employed">Self-Employed</option>
      <option value="unemployed">Unemployed</option>
    </select>

    <!-- Conditional field -->
    <div id="company-group" hidden>
      <label for="company">Company Name</label>
      <input type="text" id="company" name="company">
    </div>

    <div class="form-actions">
      <button type="button" class="btn-next">Next</button>
    </div>
  </fieldset>

  <!-- Step 2: Address -->
  <fieldset class="form-step" data-step="2" hidden>
    <legend>Address Information</legend>
    <!-- Address fields... -->
    <div class="form-actions">
      <button type="button" class="btn-prev">Back</button>
      <button type="button" class="btn-next">Next</button>
    </div>
  </fieldset>

  <!-- Step 3: Review -->
  <fieldset class="form-step" data-step="3" hidden>
    <legend>Review Your Information</legend>
    <div class="review-summary" aria-live="polite"></div>
    <div class="form-actions">
      <button type="button" class="btn-prev">Back</button>
      <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </div>
  </fieldset>
</form>
questions.interviewTip: Discuss state management strategies: each step can be a component with its own validation state. Use the browser's History API or URL hash to support browser back/forward navigation. Mention that screen reader users need clear announcements when steps change — use aria-live="polite" or role="status" for dynamic content regions.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the lang attribute and how does it affect accessibility and SEO?
questions.description:
The lang Attribute

The lang attribute specifies the primary language of the element's content. It should be set on the <html> element and can be overridden on child elements for multilingual content.

Impact

  • Screen Readers: Switch to the appropriate pronunciation rules and voice profile
  • Translation Tools: Detect the language and offer or suppress translation
  • Search Engines: Understand the language of content for language-specific search results
  • Browsers: Provide appropriate hyphenation, quotation marks, and spell-checking
questions.bestPractices:
• Always include lang on the <html> element
  • Use valid BCP 47 language tags (e.g., en, en-US, zh-Hans)
  • Override lang on elements containing content in a different language
  • Set lang on <html> even if the page has no other content
questions.commonMistakes:
• Omitting the lang attribute entirely
  • Using non-standard language codes (e.g., en_US instead of en-US)
  • Not marking language changes within multilingual content
  • Confusing lang with dir (text direction)
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en-US">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Language Example</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>This is English content.</p>

  <blockquote lang="fr">
    <p>Je ne parle pas français.</p>
  </blockquote>

  <p>As we say in Japanese:
    <span lang="ja">こんにちは</span>
  </p>

  <!-- Right-to-left language -->
  <blockquote lang="ar" dir="rtl">
    <p>مرحبا بالعالم</p>
  </blockquote>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Mention that screen readers like JAWS and NVDA have language detection and can switch voice profiles automatically. In multilingual contexts, the WCAG Success Criterion 3.1.1 (Language of Page) and 3.1.2 (Language of Parts) require proper language identification at Level A and AA respectively.

questions.title: What is the difference between block-level and inline elements? How has HTML5 changed this categorization?
questions.description:
Block-Level vs Inline Elements

Traditionally, HTML elements were categorized as block-level or inline based on their default display behavior. HTML5 has moved away from this binary classification to a more nuanced content model.

Traditional Distinction

  • Block-Level: Takes full width available, starts on a new line, can contain other block and inline elements. Examples: <div>, <p>, <h1>-<h6>, <ul>, <section>
  • Inline: Takes only necessary width, does not start a new line, flows within text. Examples: <span>, <a>, <strong>, <em>, <img>

HTML5 Content Categories

HTML5 defines categories like flow content, phrasing content, sectioning content, heading content, embedded content, and interactive content. These are more descriptive than the block/inline binary.
questions.bestPractices:
• Use CSS display property to change element behavior rather than choosing elements based on default display
  • Understand that the block/inline distinction is a CSS concept now, not an HTML specification concept
  • Use semantic elements based on meaning, not default visual behavior
questions.commonMistakes:
• Placing block-level elements inside inline elements (e.g., <div> inside <span>)
  • Assuming all elements are either block or inline — <li> has display: list-item
  • Not realizing that <a> can wrap block-level elements in HTML5
questions.example:
<!-- Block elements take full width -->
<div>This is a block element</div>
<p>This paragraph is also block-level</p>

<!-- Inline elements flow within text -->
<p>This paragraph contains
  <strong>bold text</strong> and
  <a href="#">a link</a> and
  <em>emphasized text</em>.
</p>

<!-- HTML5: a can wrap block elements -->
<a href="/article">
  <h2>Article Title</h2>
  <p>Article description...</p>
</a>
questions.interviewTip: The key insight is that HTML5 replaced the simplistic block/inline categorization with a richer content model. However, the block/inline concept is still valid in CSS (display: block vs display: inline). Mention that HTML5 allows <a> to wrap block-level elements, which was invalid in HTML4. This is useful for making entire cards clickable.

questions.title: What are void (self-closing) elements in HTML? List common void elements and their correct usage.
questions.description:
Void Elements

Void elements are HTML elements that cannot have any child nodes (i.e., nested elements or text content). They are also called self-closing or empty elements. In HTML5, the trailing slash is optional and has no effect.

Common Void Elements

  • <br> - Line break
  • <hr> - Thematic break (horizontal rule)
  • <img> - Image
  • <input> - Form input
  • <link> - External resource link
  • <meta> - Metadata
  • <source> - Media source for picture/video/audio
  • <area> - Image map area
  • <base> - Base URL
  • <col> - Table column
  • <embed> - External content embed
questions.bestPractices:
• In HTML5, write void elements without the trailing slash: <br> not <br />
  • Never attempt to nest content inside void elements
  • Use <br> only for line breaks that are part of the content (poetry, addresses)
  • Avoid <br> for spacing — use CSS margin/padding instead
questions.commonMistakes:
• Trying to add content or children to void elements: <br>text</br> is invalid
  • Using closing tags on void elements: <input type="text"></input>
  • Confusing void elements with elements that can be empty but have closing tags (e.g., <div></div>)
  • Using <br> for visual spacing instead of CSS
questions.example:
<!-- Correct HTML5 void element usage -->
<br>
<hr>
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A landscape photo">
<input type="text" name="username">
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

<!-- The trailing slash is optional in HTML5 -->
<br /> <!-- Valid but unnecessary -->
<hr /> <!-- Valid but unnecessary -->

<!-- Incorrect usage -->
<!-- <br>Some text</br> --> <!-- INVALID -->
<!-- <input type="text">Content</input> --> <!-- INVALID -->
questions.interviewTip: Mention that the trailing slash convention comes from XHTML and is still commonly seen in React JSX (where all elements must close). In standard HTML5, it's optional. The key rule: void elements cannot have content — they represent a point in the document, not a container.

questions.title: Explain the difference between the defer and async attributes on script elements. When would you use each?
questions.description:
Script Loading: defer vs async

The defer and async attributes control how external scripts are fetched and executed, impacting page load performance and script execution order.

Loading Behaviors

AttributeDownloadExecution TimingOrder Guaranteed?
None (default)Blocks parsingImmediately when downloadedYes (document order)
deferParallel to parsingAfter HTML parsing, before DOMContentLoadedYes (document order)
asyncParallel to parsingAs soon as downloaded (may interrupt parsing)No (first downloaded, first executed)
questions.bestPractices:
• Use defer for scripts that depend on the DOM and need execution order preserved
  • Use async for independent scripts (analytics, ads) where execution order doesn't matter
  • Place <script> tags in <head> when using defer or async
  • For inline scripts, use type="module" which is deferred by default
questions.commonMistakes:
• Placing scripts at the end of body AND using defer (unnecessary)
  • Using async for interdependent scripts
  • Assuming async scripts won't block rendering (they can block if they execute during parsing)
  • Forgetting that DOMContentLoaded fires after deferred scripts execute
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Script Loading</title>

  <!-- Deferred: Executes in order after HTML parsing -->
  <script src="framework.js" defer></script>
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- Async: Executes as soon as downloaded, order not guaranteed -->
  <script src="analytics.js" async></script>
  <script src="ads.js" async></script>

  <!-- Module scripts are deferred by default -->
  <script type="module" src="module-app.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
  <div id="app"></div>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Explain the performance implications: default scripts block HTML parsing, causing longer Time to Interactive. defer is generally the preferred approach for app scripts because it preserves order and waits for DOM. async is ideal for third-party scripts that don't depend on your DOM or other scripts. Mention the event sequence: DOMContentLoaded waits for deferred scripts but NOT for async scripts.

What happens if a script has both defer and async attributes?

questions.title: How does the browser parse and render an HTML page? Describe the Critical Rendering Path.
questions.description:
Critical Rendering Path

The Critical Rendering Path (CRP) is the sequence of steps the browser takes to convert HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels on the screen. Optimizing this path is crucial for fast page loads.

Steps in the CRP

  1. Build DOM: Parse HTML and construct the Document Object Model tree
  2. Build CSSOM: Parse CSS and construct the CSS Object Model tree
  3. Render Tree: Combine DOM and CSSOM into a render tree (visible elements with computed styles)
  4. Layout: Calculate the exact position and size of each element (also called reflow)
  5. Paint: Convert the layout into actual pixels on the screen
questions.bestPractices:
• Minimize render-blocking resources (CSS and synchronous JavaScript)
  • Use defer or async for non-critical JavaScript
  • Inline critical CSS for above-the-fold content
  • Use media queries on <link> to make CSS non-render-blocking when appropriate
  • Minimize the number of critical resources, critical bytes, and critical path length
questions.commonMistakes:
• Placing blocking <script> tags before the body content
  • Loading large CSS files synchronously for all media types
  • Not understanding that CSS is render-blocking by default
  • Assuming async scripts never block rendering
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <!-- Render-blocking CSS -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="critical.css">

  <!-- Non-render-blocking CSS (print only) -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="print.css" media="print">

  <!-- Non-render-blocking conditional CSS -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="mobile.css"
        media="screen and (max-width: 600px)">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Critical Rendering Path Demo</h1>
  <div id="app"></div>

  <!-- Non-render-blocking script -->
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- This script blocks rendering -->
  <script src="blocking.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Walk through the sequence: HTML parser builds DOM incrementally. When it hits a CSS link, it must download and parse CSSOM before rendering. When it hits a synchronous script, it stops DOM construction, downloads and executes the script (which may modify DOM/CSSOM), then resumes. Deferred scripts wait for DOM completion. The render tree excludes invisible elements (display:none, head). Paint happens in layers that can be composited by the GPU.
followUpQuestions: What makes a resource 'render-blocking'?
How does the browser handle an external CSS file during parsing?
What is the difference between layout and paint?
How do media queries on link elements affect rendering?
What is the role of the compositor thread in rendering?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the preload, prefetch, and preconnect resource hints in HTML?
questions.description:
Resource Hints

Resource hints tell the browser about resources that will be needed soon, allowing it to set up early connections or start downloading before they're actually requested.

Key Resource Hints

  • <link rel="preload"> - High-priority download for resources needed on the current page (fonts, hero images, critical JS/CSS)
  • <link rel="prefetch"> - Low-priority download for resources likely needed for future navigation
  • <link rel="preconnect"> - Early connection to a cross-origin (DNS, TCP, TLS handshake) before the request
  • <link rel="dns-prefetch"> - DNS resolution only for a domain
  • <link rel="modulepreload"> - Preloads ES module scripts
questions.bestPractices:
• Use preload for critical fonts, hero images, and late-discovered resources
  • Use preconnect for third-party origins (CDNs, APIs, font services)
  • Use prefetch for resources on the next page the user is likely to visit
  • Always test preload with browser DevTools — overuse can harm performance
  • Include as attribute with preload to specify resource type
questions.commonMistakes:
• Preloading too many resources, which can delay more critical ones
  • Preloading resources that aren't used on the current page (wasted bandwidth)
  • Forgetting the as attribute on preload, causing double downloads
  • Using preload for resources that change frequently without cache busting
questions.example:
<head>
  <!-- Preconnect to critical third-party origins -->
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

  <!-- Preload critical font -->
  <link rel="preload"
        href="/fonts/main-font.woff2"
        as="font"
        type="font/woff2"
        crossorigin>

  <!-- Preload hero image for LCP optimization -->
  <link rel="preload"
        href="/images/hero.webp"
        as="image"
        type="image/webp">

  <!-- Prefetch for next page navigation -->
  <link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.html" as="document">

  <!-- DNS prefetch for domains not yet needed -->
  <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://api.example.com">

  <!-- Normal stylesheet link -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css">
</head>
questions.interviewTip: Distinguish between these clearly: preconnect opens the connection early (reduces latency by ~100-300ms per origin). preload is a declarative fetch for the current page that tells the browser 'this resource is important, get it now'. prefetch is for future navigations and runs at lowest priority. Use Chrome DevTools Network waterfall to verify preconnect/preload are working correctly.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between preload and prefetch?
Why is the as attribute required on preload links?
How does preconnect improve performance for third-party resources?
What are the risks of overusing preload?

questions.title: How does the browser's speculative parsing (lookahead parser) work and why is it important for performance?
questions.description:
Speculative Parsing

The speculative parser (also called preload scanner or lookahead parser) is a secondary HTML parser that runs in parallel with the main parser. It scans ahead to discover external resources (scripts, stylesheets, images, fonts) and starts downloading them before the main parser reaches them.

How It Works

  • Runs as a lightweight, non-blocking parser
  • Scans the raw HTML bytes for resource URLs (src, href attributes)
  • Does NOT execute JavaScript or build DOM nodes
  • Starts downloading discovered resources immediately
  • Runs even when the main parser is blocked by a script
questions.bestPractices:
• Place resource hints (preload, preconnect) early in the document for the speculative parser to find
  • Avoid hiding resources behind JavaScript — the speculative parser can't see them
  • Use standard HTML attributes (src, href) for critical resources so they're discoverable
  • Test with browser DevTools to ensure critical resources are discovered early
questions.commonMistakes:
• Injecting critical CSS or images via JavaScript, making them invisible to the speculative parser
  • Using inline styles with url() that the preload scanner may not detect
  • Assuming lazy-loaded images are discovered by the speculative parser
  • Relying on the speculative parser to find resources in dynamically added HTML
questions.example:
<!-- The speculative parser discovers these immediately -->
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
  <link rel="preload" href="hero.jpg" as="image">
</head>

<body>
  <img src="logo.png" alt="Logo"> <!-- Discovered by speculative parser -->

  <script>
    // NOT discoverable by speculative parser:
    // Dynamically created elements are invisible to the preload scanner
    const img = document.createElement('img');
    img.src = 'dynamic-image.jpg'; // Not preloaded
    document.body.appendChild(img);
  </script>

  <img src="footer-banner.jpg" alt="Banner">
  <!-- Discovered even though it's at the bottom -->
</body>
questions.interviewTip: The speculative parser is a major reason why placing scripts at the bottom of the body was a popular pattern — the scanner could discover and start loading body images while the scripts executed. Modern best practices use defer/async in the head instead. Mention that the preload scanner is why resource hints (preload, preconnect) should be in the HTML source, not injected by JavaScript.
followUpQuestions: What resources can the speculative parser discover?
Why can't the speculative parser execute JavaScript?
How does the speculative parser interact with the main HTML parser?
How do resource hints complement the speculative parser?
Why are dynamically injected images slower to load than static HTML images?

questions.title: Explain the base element and its implications for relative URLs and security.
questions.description:
The Base Element

The <base> element specifies the base URL to use for all relative URLs in a document. There can be only one <base> element, and it must appear in the <head> before any elements with relative URLs.

Attributes

  • href - The base URL for all relative URLs in the document
  • target - Default target for hyperlinks and forms (_blank, _self, _parent, _top)
questions.bestPractices:
• Use <base> sparingly — it has global side effects that can be hard to debug
  • If used, place it before any elements that use relative URLs
  • Be aware that it affects ALL relative URLs including anchors, images, scripts, stylesheets, and form actions
  • Consider using absolute URLs or a build-time URL prefix instead
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using multiple <base> elements (only the first one is honored)
  • Placing <base> after links or scripts that use relative URLs
  • Forgetting that <base> also affects fragment-only links (href="#section")
  • Unintentionally changing form submission targets with the target attribute
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <base href="https://example.com/app/" target="_blank">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles/main.css">
  <!-- Resolves to: https://example.com/app/styles/main.css -->
</head>
<body>
  <img src="images/logo.png" alt="Logo">
  <!-- Resolves to: https://example.com/app/images/logo.png -->

  <a href="about">About</a>
  <!-- Navigates to https://example.com/app/about in new tab -->

  <a href="#section">Jump to section</a>
  <!-- Also resolves against base! Navigates to https://example.com/app/#section -->

  <form action="submit">
    <!-- Submits to https://example.com/app/submit in new tab -->
  </form>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Highlight the security implication: if an attacker can inject a <base> tag (via XSS or content injection), they can redirect all relative URLs to a malicious domain. This is why Content Security Policy (CSP) with base-uri directive is important. Also mention that fragment links (#section) become full navigations with a base URL, which can break single-page app behavior.

What are alternatives to using the base element?

questions.title: What is Content Security Policy (CSP) and how do you implement it via HTML meta tags?
questions.description:
Content Security Policy

Content Security Policy (CSP) is a security layer that helps detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. It can be delivered via HTTP headers or <meta> tags.

Key Directives

  • default-src - Default source for all resource types
  • script-src - Allowed sources for JavaScript
  • style-src - Allowed sources for CSS
  • img-src - Allowed sources for images
  • connect-src - Allowed targets for fetch/XHR/WebSocket
  • font-src - Allowed sources for fonts
  • frame-src - Allowed sources for frames
  • base-uri - Allowed URLs for base element
  • form-action - Allowed targets for form submissions
questions.bestPractices:
• Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header to test without breaking functionality
  • Use nonces or hashes for inline scripts instead of 'unsafe-inline'
  • Set via HTTP header when possible (meta tag supports fewer directives)
  • Gradually tighten the policy as you identify all legitimate resource sources
  • Use CSP evaluator tools to check for policy weaknesses
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using 'unsafe-inline' which undermines CSP's XSS protection
  • Forgetting to include sources for all resource types used on the page
  • Not testing in report-only mode before enforcing
  • Setting CSP only via meta tag, missing some header-only directives
questions.example:
<head>
  <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
        content="default-src 'self';
                 script-src 'self' 'nonce-random123' https://trusted-cdn.com;
                 style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://fonts.googleapis.com;
                 img-src 'self' https: data:;
                 font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com;
                 connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com;
                 frame-src 'none';
                 base-uri 'self';
                 form-action 'self';
                 upgrade-insecure-requests;">
</head>

<script nonce="random123">
  // This inline script is allowed because it has the correct nonce
  console.log('CSP-compliant inline script');
</script>
questions.interviewTip: Emphasize the limitations of meta tag CSP: report-uri and frame-ancestors directives are not supported in meta tags. For full CSP control, use HTTP headers. Explain the nonce approach: a unique, unpredictable value is generated per request and placed both in the CSP header and on allowed script tags. This allows specific inline scripts without using 'unsafe-inline'.

How does script nonce work to allow inline scripts?

questions.title: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and how can HTML-level protections help prevent it?
questions.description:
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

XSS attacks inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. HTML-level protections, combined with proper server-side handling, form a defense-in-depth strategy against XSS.

Types of XSS

  • Stored XSS: Malicious script stored on server (database, comments)
  • Reflected XSS: Malicious script reflected off server (search results, error messages)
  • DOM-based XSS: Vulnerability in client-side JavaScript manipulating DOM unsafely

HTML-Level Protections

  • Output Encoding: Encode HTML entities (< for <) when inserting user data
  • CSP: Restrict script sources and block inline scripts
  • Sanitization: Use libraries like DOMPurify to clean HTML input
  • Safe DOM APIs: Use textContent instead of innerHTML for text
questions.bestPractices:
• Always encode user-generated content before rendering in HTML
  • Use textContent or innerText instead of innerHTML when inserting text
  • Validate and sanitize all user inputs on both client and server
  • Implement CSP to block inline scripts and restrict script sources
  • Avoid using eval(), setTimeout with strings, new Function()
questions.commonMistakes:
• Trusting user input and inserting it directly into the DOM with innerHTML
  • Relying only on client-side validation
  • Forgetting to encode data in HTML attributes (especially event handlers and href)
  • Using blacklists instead of allowlists for HTML sanitization
  • Thinking that escaping single/double quotes is sufficient for all contexts
questions.example:
<!-- VULNERABLE: Direct insertion of user data -->
<div id="user-comment">
  <!-- <script>alert('XSS')</script> would execute -->
</div>

<!-- SAFE: Using textContent -->
<script>
  const comment = document.getElementById('user-comment');
  // Safe: treated as text, not parsed as HTML
  comment.textContent = userInput;

  // Unsafe: userInput is parsed as HTML
  // comment.innerHTML = userInput; // DON'T DO THIS
</script>

<!-- SAFE: HTML encoding on the server -->
<div>
  <script>alert('XSS')</script>
  <!-- Renders as text, not executed -->
</div>

<!-- SAFE: Using DOMPurify for rich text -->
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/dompurify/dist/purify.min.js">
</script>
<script>
  const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(userHTML);
  comment.innerHTML = clean; // Only safe HTML tags remain
</script>
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the importance of context-aware encoding: HTML entity encoding for HTML body, attribute encoding for attributes, JavaScript encoding for script blocks, and URL encoding for href/src. Each context requires different encoding rules. Mention the Trusted Types API as an emerging browser feature to prevent DOM XSS at the platform level.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between Stored, Reflected, and DOM-based XSS?
How does DOMPurify sanitize HTML safely?

Why is innerHTML dangerous compared to textContent?

questions.title: What is iframe sandboxing and how do the sandbox attribute values work?
questions.description:
Iframe Sandboxing

The sandbox attribute on <iframe> applies restrictions to content within the iframe, creating a secure environment for untrusted content. By default, the sandbox applies all restrictions.

Sandbox Tokens (Lift Restrictions)

  • allow-scripts - Allow JavaScript execution
  • allow-same-origin - Treat iframe content as same origin (enables cookies, localStorage)
  • allow-forms - Allow form submission
  • allow-popups - Allow popups (window.open)
  • allow-top-navigation - Allow navigating the top-level browsing context
  • allow-modals - Allow modal dialogs (alert, confirm, prompt)
  • allow-downloads - Allow downloads
  • allow-pointer-lock - Allow Pointer Lock API
questions.bestPractices:
• Always use the sandbox attribute for untrusted content (ads, user-generated content)
  • Apply least-privilege: only add tokens that are absolutely necessary
  • Never combine allow-scripts with allow-same-origin on untrusted content
  • Also set loading="lazy" for performance
questions.commonMistakes:
• Using iframes without sandbox for untrusted content
  • Combining allow-scripts and allow-same-origin (scripts can remove sandbox attribute entirely)
  • Forgetting to add necessary tokens, causing functional issues
  • Assuming sandbox alone prevents all attacks (it's one layer of defense)
questions.example:
<!-- Maximum restriction (no permissions) -->
<iframe src="untrusted-content.html"
        sandbox=""
        title="Sandboxed content">
</iframe>

<!-- Allow scripts and forms, but not same-origin -->
<iframe src="widget.html"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"
        title="Interactive widget">
</iframe>

<!-- For trusted same-origin content -->
<iframe src="/trusted-app.html"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms"
        title="Trusted application">
</iframe>

<!-- YouTube embed with necessary permissions -->
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/videoId"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-presentation"
        allow="accelerometer; autoplay; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture"
        allowfullscreen
        title="YouTube video player">
</iframe>
questions.interviewTip: Critical security point: if you include both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin, the sandbox is effectively useless. With same-origin, scripts can access the iframe's own document and remove the sandbox attribute. Always keep these two tokens separate for untrusted content. Also mention the allow attribute for Feature Policy/Permissions Policy, which controls access to browser features like camera, microphone, etc.
followUpQuestions: Why shouldn't allow-scripts and allow-same-origin be used together?
What is the difference between sandbox and the allow attribute?
How does the sandbox attribute affect iframe performance?
What happens if you set sandbox without any tokens?
How do you communicate between an iframe and its parent securely?

questions.title: Explain the role of the viewport meta tag in responsive web design.
questions.description:
Viewport Meta Tag

The viewport meta tag instructs the browser how to control the page's dimensions and scaling on different devices. Without it, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop width and scale it down, making text unreadable.

Common Configuration

  • width=device-width - Sets the viewport width to the device's screen width
  • initial-scale=1.0 - Sets the initial zoom level when the page first loads
  • maximum-scale - Limits how much users can zoom in
  • minimum-scale - Limits how much users can zoom out
  • user-scalable - Whether users can zoom at all (yes or no)
questions.bestPractices:
• Always include <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  • Avoid disabling user scaling (user-scalable=no) — it harms accessibility
  • Avoid setting maximum-scale=1.0 — it prevents users with visual impairments from zooming
  • Use CSS media queries for responsive breakpoints, not viewport hackery
questions.commonMistakes:
• Omitting the viewport meta tag entirely
  • Disabling user zoom with user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1.0
  • Setting a fixed width like width=1024 instead of device-width
  • Including the viewport tag twice with conflicting values
questions.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">

  <!-- Recommended responsive viewport -->
  <meta name="viewport"
        content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

  <!-- AVOID: Disables zoom, harms accessibility -->
  <!-- <meta name="viewport"
           content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0,
                    maximum-scale=1.0, user-scalable=no"> -->

  <title>Responsive Page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>This page works on all devices</h1>
</body>
</html>
questions.interviewTip: Discuss the WCAG accessibility requirement: Success Criterion 1.4.4 (Resize Text) requires that text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content. Disabling zoom violates this. Also mention that iOS Safari introduced 'viewport shrinking' in iOS 9 to handle desktop-width pages, but the viewport meta tag is still essential for proper responsive behavior.

How does the viewport meta tag affect media queries?
What is the default viewport width on mobile browsers without this tag?
How do you handle the viewport for tablets vs phones?
What is viewport-fit=cover used for in notched devices?

questions.title: What are media queries and how can they be used within HTML for responsive design?
questions.description:
Media Queries in HTML

Media queries allow you to conditionally apply styles or load resources based on device characteristics like viewport width, height, orientation, resolution, and user preferences.

Usage in HTML

  • Link element: <link rel="stylesheet" media="(condition)" href="...">
  • Style element: <style media="(condition)">
  • Source element: <source media="(condition)" srcset="...">
  • Picture element: Art direction based on media queries
questions.bestPractices:
• Use media queries on <link> to prevent render-blocking for non-matching stylesheets
  • Combine with resource hints for optimal loading
  • Use prefers-reduced-motion to respect user accessibility preferences
  • Use prefers-color-scheme for dark mode support
questions.commonMistakes:
• Not specifying a media attribute on link elements, causing unconditional loading
  • Using only width-based media queries without considering other device features
  • Forgetting that media queries on link elements can improve performance (non-matching stylesheets are downloaded at low priority)
questions.example:
<head>
  <!-- Conditional stylesheet loading -->
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="mobile.css"
        media="screen and (max-width: 767px)">

  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="desktop.css"
        media="screen and (min-width: 768px)">

  <!-- Print stylesheet -->
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="print.css"
        media="print">

  <!-- Responsive images with picture -->
  <picture>
    <source media="(min-width: 1024px)"
            srcset="hero-large.webp">
    <source media="(min-width: 768px)"
            srcset="hero-medium.webp">
    <img src="hero-small.webp"
         alt="Responsive hero image">
  </picture>

  <style media="(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)">
    * {
      animation: none !important;
      transition: none !important;
    }
  </style>

  <style media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
    body {
      background-color: #1a1a1a;
      color: #ffffff;
    }
  </style>
</head>
questions.interviewTip: Key performance insight: Browsers load all stylesheets regardless of media queries, but non-matching ones are loaded at low priority and don't block rendering. This is different from using display:none in CSS — the file is still downloaded. Use media queries on link elements strategically to improve perceived performance.

What are user preference media queries like prefers-reduced-motion?
